Techniques
○ Do nothing well - Most microprocessors turn off the clock of inactive modules to save energy
and dynamic power
○ Dynamic Voltage-Frequency Scaling (DVFS)
○ Design for typical case - PMDs and laptops are often idle, memory and storage offer low
power modes to save energy. E.g., DRAMs different increasingly lower power modes to extend
battery life, so disks can spin at lower rates when idle. You cannot access DRAMs or disks in
these modes, so must return to fully active mode to read or write.
○ Overclocking - Operate single core at higher clock rate. Risk of overheating ^1W4UMonp

Flynn’s Taxonomy - Founded in the 1960s
● Single instruction stream, single data stream (SISD)
○ Uni-processor. Sequential computer but can exploit instruction-level parallelism. Use ILP techs (superscalar and
speculative execution).
● Single instruction stream, multiple data streams (SIMD)
○ The same instruction is executed by multiple processors using different data streams. Exploit data-level parallelism
by applying the same operations to multiple items of data in parallel.
○ Each processor has its own data memory (hence the MD of SIMD), but there is a single instruction memory and
control processor.
○ DLP and three different architectures that exploit it: vector architectures, multimedia extensions to standard
instruction sets, and GPUs.
● Multiple instruction streams, single data stream (MISD)
○ No commercial multiprocessor of this type has been built to date.
● Multiple instruction streams, multiple data streams (MIMD)
○ Each processor fetches its own instructions and operates on its own data, targeting task-level parallelism.
○ More flexible than SIMD and thus more generally applicable, but more expensive.
○ Tightly coupled MIMD - exploit thread-level parallelism since multiple cooperating threads operate in parallel;
Loosely coupled MIMD – (clusters and warehouse-scale computers) exploit request-level parallelism with little
communication or synchronization.

● The Myopic View: only Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)
○ ISA serves as the boundary between the software and hardware
○ Seven dimensions: Class of ISA, Memory addressing, Addressing modes, Types and sizes
of operands, Operations, Control flow instructions, and Encoding an ISA
● The Genuine: Designing the Organization and Hardware
○ Meet functional requirements as well as price, power, performance, and availability
goals.
○ Cover three aspects: Instruction set architecture, Microarchitecture Addressing modes,

Caching data: read is easy as the copy in the cache and memory will be
identical; write is more difficult, e.g., copy in the cache and memory be
kept consistent?

● Two main strategies: write-through cache and write-back
○ write-through: updates the item in the cache and writes through to update
main memory
○ write-back: only updates the copy in the cache. When the block is about to be
replaced, it is copied back to memory

○ Both can use a buffer to allow the cache to proceed as soon as the data are
placed in the buffer rather than wait the full latency to write the data into
memory. One measure of the benefits of different cache organizations is miss
rate ^QaqVEUEE

			"fontSize": 16,
			"fontFamily": 5,
			"text": "•Data movement instructions move information from the processing unit to and \nfrom memory and to and from input/output devices. ",
			"textAlign": "left",
			"verticalAlign": "top",
			"containerId": null,
			"originalText": "•Data movement instructions move information from the processing unit to and from memory and to and from input/output devices. ",

			"fontSize": 16,
			"fontFamily": 5,
			"text": "•Control instructions are necessary for altering the sequential processing \nof instructions.",
			"textAlign": "left",
			"verticalAlign": "top",
			"containerId": null,
			"originalText": "•Control instructions are necessary for altering the sequential processing of instructions.",

			"fontSize": 16,
			"fontFamily": 5,
			"text": "normally the instructions would be executed in the sequence 1,2,3...10. \nHowever, sometimes we will want to change the sequence. Control instructions\nenable us to do that.",
			"textAlign": "left",
			"verticalAlign": "top",
			"containerId": null,
			"originalText": "normally the instructions would be executed in the sequence 1,2,3...10. However, sometimes we will want to change the sequence. Control instructions enable us to do that.",

			"lineHeight": 1.25
		},

			"text": "That is, normally the next instruction executed is the instruction \ncontained in the next memory location. If a program consists of \ninstructions 1,2,3,4...10 located in memory locations A, A+1, A+2, ...A+9,",
			"textAlign": "left",

			"fontSize": 16,
			"fontFamily": 5,
			"text": "Techniques\n○ Do nothing well - Most microprocessors turn off the clock of inactive modules to save energy\nand dynamic power\n○ Dynamic Voltage-Frequency Scaling (DVFS)\n○ Design for typical case - PMDs and laptops are often idle, memory and storage offer low\npower modes to save energy. E.g., DRAMs different increasingly lower power modes to extend\nbattery life, so disks can spin at lower rates when idle. You cannot access DRAMs or disks in\nthese modes, so must return to fully active mode to read or write.\n○ Overclocking - Operate single core at higher clock rate. Risk of overheating",
			"textAlign": "left",
			"verticalAlign": "top",
			"containerId": null,
			"originalText": "Techniques\n○ Do nothing well - Most microprocessors turn off the clock of inactive modules to save energy\nand dynamic power\n○ Dynamic Voltage-Frequency Scaling (DVFS)\n○ Design for typical case - PMDs and laptops are often idle, memory and storage offer low\npower modes to save energy. E.g., DRAMs different increasingly lower power modes to extend\nbattery life, so disks can spin at lower rates when idle. You cannot access DRAMs or disks in\nthese modes, so must return to fully active mode to read or write.\n○ Overclocking - Operate single core at higher clock rate. Risk of overheating",
			"autoResize": true,
			"lineHeight": 1.25
		},

		{
			"type": "text",
			"version": 81,

			"y": -4614.88658828392,

			"updated": 1725071255215,
			"link": null,
			"locked": false,
			"fontSize": 16,
			"fontFamily": 5,
			"text": "Flynn’s Taxonomy - Founded in the 1960s\n● Single instruction stream, single data stream (SISD)\n○ Uni-processor. Sequential computer but can exploit instruction-level parallelism. Use ILP techs (superscalar and\nspeculative execution).\n● Single instruction stream, multiple data streams (SIMD)\n○ The same instruction is executed by multiple processors using different data streams. Exploit data-level parallelism\nby applying the same operations to multiple items of data in parallel.\n○ Each processor has its own data memory (hence the MD of SIMD), but there is a single instruction memory and\ncontrol processor.\n○ DLP and three different architectures that exploit it: vector architectures, multimedia extensions to standard\ninstruction sets, and GPUs.\n● Multiple instruction streams, single data stream (MISD)\n○ No commercial multiprocessor of this type has been built to date.\n● Multiple instruction streams, multiple data streams (MIMD)\n○ Each processor fetches its own instructions and operates on its own data, targeting task-level parallelism.\n○ More flexible than SIMD and thus more generally applicable, but more expensive.\n○ Tightly coupled MIMD - exploit thread-level parallelism since multiple cooperating threads operate in parallel;\nLoosely coupled MIMD – (clusters and warehouse-scale computers) exploit request-level parallelism with little\ncommunication or synchronization.\n\n● The Myopic View: only Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)\n○ ISA serves as the boundary between the software and hardware\n○ Seven dimensions: Class of ISA, Memory addressing, Addressing modes, Types and sizes\nof operands, Operations, Control flow instructions, and Encoding an ISA\n● The Genuine: Designing the Organization and Hardware\n○ Meet functional requirements as well as price, power, performance, and availability\ngoals.\n○ Cover three aspects: Instruction set architecture, Microarchitecture Addressing modes,\nHardware",
			"textAlign": "left",
			"verticalAlign": "top",
			"containerId": null,
			"originalText": "Flynn’s Taxonomy - Founded in the 1960s\n● Single instruction stream, single data stream (SISD)\n○ Uni-processor. Sequential computer but can exploit instruction-level parallelism. Use ILP techs (superscalar and\nspeculative execution).\n● Single instruction stream, multiple data streams (SIMD)\n○ The same instruction is executed by multiple processors using different data streams. Exploit data-level parallelism\nby applying the same operations to multiple items of data in parallel.\n○ Each processor has its own data memory (hence the MD of SIMD), but there is a single instruction memory and\ncontrol processor.\n○ DLP and three different architectures that exploit it: vector architectures, multimedia extensions to standard\ninstruction sets, and GPUs.\n● Multiple instruction streams, single data stream (MISD)\n○ No commercial multiprocessor of this type has been built to date.\n● Multiple instruction streams, multiple data streams (MIMD)\n○ Each processor fetches its own instructions and operates on its own data, targeting task-level parallelism.\n○ More flexible than SIMD and thus more generally applicable, but more expensive.\n○ Tightly coupled MIMD - exploit thread-level parallelism since multiple cooperating threads operate in parallel;\nLoosely coupled MIMD – (clusters and warehouse-scale computers) exploit request-level parallelism with little\ncommunication or synchronization.\n\n● The Myopic View: only Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)\n○ ISA serves as the boundary between the software and hardware\n○ Seven dimensions: Class of ISA, Memory addressing, Addressing modes, Types and sizes\nof operands, Operations, Control flow instructions, and Encoding an ISA\n● The Genuine: Designing the Organization and Hardware\n○ Meet functional requirements as well as price, power, performance, and availability\ngoals.\n○ Cover three aspects: Instruction set architecture, Microarchitecture Addressing modes,\nHardware",
			"autoResize": true,
			"lineHeight": 1.25
		},

			"link": null,

			"fontSize": 16,
			"fontFamily": 5,
			"text": "Caching data: read is easy as the copy in the cache and memory will be\nidentical; write is more difficult, e.g., copy in the cache and memory be\nkept consistent?\n\n● Two main strategies: write-through cache and write-back\n○ write-through: updates the item in the cache and writes through to update\nmain memory\n○ write-back: only updates the copy in the cache. When the block is about to be\nreplaced, it is copied back to memory\n\n○ Both can use a buffer to allow the cache to proceed as soon as the data are\nplaced in the buffer rather than wait the full latency to write the data into\nmemory. One measure of the benefits of different cache organizations is miss\nrate",
			"textAlign": "left",
			"verticalAlign": "top",
			"containerId": null,
			"originalText": "Caching data: read is easy as the copy in the cache and memory will be\nidentical; write is more difficult, e.g., copy in the cache and memory be\nkept consistent?\n\n● Two main strategies: write-through cache and write-back\n○ write-through: updates the item in the cache and writes through to update\nmain memory\n○ write-back: only updates the copy in the cache. When the block is about to be\nreplaced, it is copied back to memory\n\n○ Both can use a buffer to allow the cache to proceed as soon as the data are\nplaced in the buffer rather than wait the full latency to write the data into\nmemory. One measure of the benefits of different cache organizations is miss\nrate",
